introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá expected warships to become merchant steamers and people to give their nationality as “the nationality of humanity.” The readings move between two scales. Within a country, above all the Iran of the constitutional revolution, government and people must “mix like honey and milk.” Among countries there must be a tribunal, a league that represents all, and at last a commonwealth; the League of 1920 is “only the merest beginning.” The hope is old and has had many spokesmen, and they are here: Isaiah’s plowshares, Diogenes the citizen of the world, Zeno’s one polity, Tennyson’s Parliament of man, Hugo’s United States of Europe, Wilson’s fourteenth point, the Universal Declaration. So are the people who doubted it or feared it: Burke on the little platoon, Jefferson on entangling alliances, Kant on a world state as soulless despotism, Mill on minds moulded alike, Tacitus on the peace of the strong, and the Athenians at Melos.
questions: “To which nationality do you belong?” Burke says love of mankind begins in “the little platoon.” Do the readings ask that smaller loyalties be given up, widened, or kept in their place?

The readings call for a league “for the government of the world” and speak of a world commonwealth. Kant wanted a federation but feared a universal state. Which of the safeguards in the last readings answer him, and which of his worries remain?
“Until government and nation mix together like honey and milk, success … [is] impossible.” Mencius puts the people first; the Declaration speaks of consent. What kind of mixing do the readings mean?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says peace needs a conference “under the influence of the Word of God”; UNESCO says the defences of peace must be built in the minds of men. Are these the same claim?
Tacitus’s chief and the Athenians at Melos describe peace as the strong impose it. What in these readings distinguishes universal peace from that?
Hugo spoke of a United States of Europe in 1849 and the readings in the 1910s. What has happened since, and what does the history suggest about how such hopes are realized?

outside.why: Asked their nationality, the people of the future will answer “the nationality of humanity.” Diogenes, asked where he came from, gave the first such answer on record: I am a citizen of the world.

National names are to fall away. Burke held that love of mankind is learned in smaller loyalties: to love the little platoon we belong to in society is the first link in the series by which we proceed towards a love to our country and to mankind. Can the larger loyalty live without the smaller ones?
“These warships will be changed into merchant steamers.” Isaiah’s version, carved today outside the United Nations: they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks.
“Humanity has become interdependent.” Martin Luther King, from a jail in Birmingham: we are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny.
Problems and their results are now universal. Donne, in a sickroom in 1623: no man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main.
Serve your country “in your capacity as a citizen of the world.” The motto William Lloyd Garrison printed on his newspaper: our country is the world, our countrymen are all mankind.

Federalism is to be extended to the relations of nations. Jefferson’s first inaugural set the opposite course for the federal republic itself: peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none. What changed between 1801 and the age of the readings?

While blood is spilled in the Balkans, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes for “the banner of universal peace.” Tennyson in 1842: till the war-drum throbbed no longer, and the battle-flags were furled in the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.
“The true duty of a powerful king is to establish a universal peace.” Jesus: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.

Peace established by the powerful “signifies the freedom of all.” A Caledonian chief in Tacitus describes the peace that the powerful of his day established: they make a desert, and they call it peace. How is the one kind told from the other?
National affairs will not go right “until the whole people have received instruction.” Proverbs: where there is no vision, the people perish.

“Public thought has been directed to a single end.” Mill feared exactly that from schooling in the hands of the state: a mere contrivance for moulding people to be exactly like one another. Who does the directing in the readings?

“A Supreme Tribunal will be established.” The last of Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points, January 1918: a general association of nations must be formed, for mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike.
If government and nation do not mix, “the great calamity shall come.” Jesus: every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation.

“Until government and nation mix together like honey and milk, success … [is] impossible.” Mencius gave the order of importance within that mixture: the people are the most important element in a nation; the sovereign is the lightest.
Iran is “outwardly calm, inwardly … turbulent” for lack of unity. Lincoln in 1858, quoting the Gospel at his own country: a house divided against itself cannot stand.
Government and people “are like vein and spirit, like body and arteries.” Menenius, in Coriolanus, calms a riot with the fable of the belly and the members that rebelled against it.

The friends are to work “so that different parties may become one party.” Washington’s Farewell Address warns his countrymen in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party.
“All are the progeny of Adam.” Malachi: have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?
Christ gathered diverse peoples “under the same canopy.” Ephesians on how: he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition.
A small association for the connection of East and West needs steadfastness. Jesus on small beginnings: a grain of mustard seed, the least of all seeds, becometh a tree.

Iran and England will give their lives for one another. Kipling’s ballad of 1889 opens with the line everyone quotes, never the twain shall meet, and goes on to the exception: when two strong men stand face to face. Is friendship between nations made of such meetings?
Peace needs a conference “working under the influence of the Word of God.” Zechariah: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.

Without that influence “it is impossible.” The founders of UNESCO, in 1945, also looked past treaties: since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.
“They say that soon the leaders of the world will … establish a universal peace celebration.” Jeremiah on leaders who announce such things: saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
“May this American democracy be the first nation.” John Winthrop gave the colony its sense of being watched in 1630: we shall be as a city upon a hill; the eyes of all people are upon us.
America is “the readiest and the freest nation to arise in the service of humanity.” The lines on the Statue of Liberty: give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.

The existing League “palliates the disease … It is no remedy.” Madison on why any government is hard to design: if men were angels, no government would be necessary. What would a league that is a remedy have to assume about nations?
The world is “shedding off its old skin.” Tennyson’s bells: ring out the old, ring in the new; ring out the thousand wars of old, ring in the thousand years of peace.

“Undreamed of changes and revolutions.” Marx and Engels described the same melting in 1848 and expected a different outcome: all that is solid melts into air, and man is at last compelled to face his real conditions of life.

Leaders must draft a plan of union that mirrors “the Realm on High.” Plato thought cities would have no rest from evils until philosophers were kings, and did not expect to see it. What do the readings rely on that he lacked?

“We are the well-wishers of both sides.” Confucius on influence that does not take sides: he who governs by virtue is like the north polar star, which keeps its place and all the stars turn towards it.

Division at home “will ultimately lead to the interference of neighboring powers.” The Athenians at Melos stated the rule those powers follow: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. Can unity within protect the weak from it?
Unity came when the Shah ordered constitutional government. The American Declaration: governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.
The unity of the American states is possible among the powers of the world. Aesop’s father shows his sons a bundle of sticks that none of them can break.

“The next natural step will be the constitution of a United States of Europe.” Victor Hugo used the very phrase at the Paris Peace Congress of 1849: a day will come when these two immense groups, the United States of America and the United States of Europe, shall be seen holding out their hands across the seas.

A yearly congress of the world’s thinkers and statesmen, meeting in Egypt. Whitman on what the age was for: the earth to be spanned, connected by network, the races, neighbours, to marry and be given in marriage, the lands to be welded together.
A “Universal Collective Center” is needed, wider than race, nation or party. Zeno the Stoic, as Plutarch reports him, asked that we consider all men to be of one community and one polity.

The partial collective centres “prevent” peace. Kant thought nature works through that very rivalry: man wills concord, but nature knows better what is good for his species; she wills discord. Is conflict among nations only an obstacle?

All peoples “citizens of one common fatherland.” The first article of the Universal Declaration: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.
A world commonwealth with a legislature, an executive and a tribunal. The Confucian Book of Rites remembers and hopes for the Grand Union, when a public and common spirit ruled all under the sky.

Shoghi Effendi’s secretary speaks of “a world superstate.” Kant, who wanted a federation of free states, feared the single world state as a soulless despotism in which laws lose their force as the government grows. How do the safeguards named in the reading meet his fear?
The commonwealth must safeguard “the personal freedom and initiative of the individuals.” Mill: the worth of a State, in the long run, is the worth of the individuals composing it.
Humanity has entered “the stage of maturity.” Paul’s figure for a people coming of age: the heir, as long as he is a child, is under tutors and governors until the time appointed.
